claim: The association between pregnancy and altered cutaneous pigmentation has been documented for over two millennia.
source: The association between pregnancy and altered cutaneous pigmentation has been documented for over two millennia, suggesting that sex hormones play a role in regulating epidermal melanocyte (MC) homeostasis.
evidence: This is a historical statement supported by citations to historical medical texts in the Introduction section.

claim: Physiologic estrogen (17β-estradiol) increases melanin synthesis.
source: Here we show that physiologic estrogen (17β-estradiol) and progesterone reciprocally regulate melanin synthesis.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Progesterone decreases melanin synthesis.
source: Here we show that physiologic estrogen (17β-estradiol) and progesterone reciprocally regulate melanin synthesis.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Normal primary human melanocytes lack classical estrogen receptors (ER).
source: This is intriguing given that we also show that normal primary human MCs lack classical estrogen or progesterone receptors (ER or PR).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, RNAseq data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, and western blot in Figure 2F.

claim: Normal primary human melanocytes lack classical progesterone receptors (PR).
source: This is intriguing given that we also show that normal primary human MCs lack classical estrogen or progesterone receptors (ER or PR).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, RNAseq data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, and western blot in Figure 2F.

claim: Sex steroid effects on human pigment synthesis are mediated by the membrane-bound G protein-coupled estrogen receptor (GPER).
source: Utilizing both genetic and pharmacologic approaches, we establish that sex steroid effects on human pigment synthesis are mediated by the membrane-bound, steroid hormone receptors G protein-coupled estrogen receptor (GPER), and progestin and adipoQ receptor 7 (PAQR7).
evidence: Supported by shRNA knockdown experiments (Figure 2G), CRISPR knockout experiments (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G), and pharmacologic agonist experiments (Figure 3A-C).

claim: Sex steroid effects on human pigment synthesis are mediated by progestin and adipoQ receptor 7 (PAQR7).
source: Utilizing both genetic and pharmacologic approaches, we establish that sex steroid effects on human pigment synthesis are mediated by the membrane-bound, steroid hormone receptors G protein-coupled estrogen receptor (GPER), and progestin and adipoQ receptor 7 (PAQR7).
evidence: Supported by shRNA knockdown experiments (Figure 2H), CRISPR knockout experiments (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H), and pharmacologic agonist experiments (Figure 3D-F).

claim: GPER and PAQR7 activity can be activated or inhibited by synthetic estrogen or progesterone analogs that do not bind to ER or PR.
source: Activity of these receptors was activated or inhibited by synthetic estrogen or progesterone analogs that do not bind to ER or PR.
evidence: Supported by experiments with G-1 (GPER agonist) shown in Figure 3A-C and CH2P4 (PAQR7 agonist) shown in Figure 3D-F.

claim: Hippocrates (460–370 B.C.E.) recognized pregnancy-associated hyperpigmentation.
source: The British physician Daniel Turner, in his 1714 De Morbis Cutaneis (Turner, 1726), references Hippocrates (460–370 B.C.E.), "There is a spot on the face…more peculiar, according to our great master Hippoc., to Big Belly'd women, and recon'd as one of the Signs of Conception."
evidence: Historical reference cited from Turner (1726).

claim: Modern physicians recognize pregnancy-associated hyperpigmentation as melasma.
source: Modern physicians recognize this common pregnancy-associated hyperpigmentation as melasma (Sheth and Pandya, 2011; Nicolaidou and Katsambas, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to medical literature.

claim: Melanocytes in the basal epidermis control skin pigmentation through synthesis of melanin.
source: Melanocytes in the basal epidermis control skin pigmentation through synthesis of melanin, a complex process thought to be primarily regulated by alpha-melanocyte stimulating hormone (αMSH) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about melanocyte function.

claim: Melanin synthesis is primarily regulated by alpha-melanocyte stimulating hormone (αMSH).
source: Melanocytes in the basal epidermis control skin pigmentation through synthesis of melanin, a complex process thought to be primarily regulated by alpha-melanocyte stimulating hormone (αMSH) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about melanin regulation.

claim: αMSH peptide is secreted centrally by the anterior pituitary gland.
source: The αMSH peptide is secreted centrally by the anterior pituitary gland, and locally by keratinocytes in response to UV damage (Cui et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cui et al., 2007.

claim: αMSH peptide is secreted locally by keratinocytes in response to UV damage.
source: The αMSH peptide is secreted centrally by the anterior pituitary gland, and locally by keratinocytes in response to UV damage (Cui et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cui et al., 2007.

claim: αMSH binding to MC1R activates adenylate cyclase and increases cAMP.
source: αMSH binding to the melanocortin receptor 1 (MC1R), a G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR), activates adenylate cyclase, and increases cAMP.
evidence: This is established knowledge about MC1R signaling pathway.

claim: cAMP activates a cascade of downstream transcriptional events leading to expression of genes required for melanin synthesis.
source: This secondary messenger activates a cascade of downstream transcriptional events leading to expression of genes required for melanin synthesis (Rodríguez and Setaluri, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rodríguez and Setaluri, 2014.

claim: Forskolin stimulates melanin production.
source: Exogenous broadly-acting adenylate cyclase activators such as plant-derived forskolin, also stimulate melanin production (D'Orazio et al., 2006), but the degree to which other endogenous molecules, other than αMSH regulate melanin synthesis in tissue is unclear.
evidence: Supported by citation to D'Orazio et al., 2006.

claim: Melasma frequently occurs in non-pregnant women using oral contraceptive pills.
source: However, the observation that melasma frequently occurs in non-pregnant women using oral contraceptive pills, which contain only steroid hormone analogs (Sheth and Pandya, 2011; Resnik, 1967a), suggests that humans may maintain αMSH-independent pigment control mechanisms.
evidence: Supported by citations to Sheth and Pandya, 2011 and Resnik, 1967a.

claim: Humans may maintain αMSH-independent pigment control mechanisms.
source: However, the observation that melasma frequently occurs in non-pregnant women using oral contraceptive pills, which contain only steroid hormone analogs (Sheth and Pandya, 2011; Resnik, 1967a), suggests that humans may maintain αMSH-independent pigment control mechanisms.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation about oral contraceptives and melasma.

claim: Treatment with 25 nM estrogen for 4 days resulted in a 208% ± 27% increase in melanin in three individual isolates of primary human melanocytes.
source: After 4 days of exposure to 25 nM estrogen, a medically-relevant concentration observed during pregnancy (Abbassi-Ghanavati et al., 2009), melanin was markedly increased (208% +/- 27%) in three individual isolates of primary human melanocytes (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: 25 nM estrogen is a medically-relevant concentration observed during pregnancy.
source: After 4 days of exposure to 25 nM estrogen, a medically-relevant concentration observed during pregnancy (Abbassi-Ghanavati et al., 2009), melanin was markedly increased (208% +/- 27%) in three individual isolates of primary human melanocytes (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by citation to Abbassi-Ghanavati et al., 2009.

claim: The magnitude of melanin increase with estrogen was similar to that observed with αMSH.
source: The magnitude of this change was similar to that observed with αMSH (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), and is consistent with prior in vitro studies implicating estrogen in melanin synthesis (McLeod et al., 1994; Ranson et al., 1988).
evidence: Supported by comparison data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Prior in vitro studies have implicated estrogen in melanin synthesis.
source: The magnitude of this change was similar to that observed with αMSH (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), and is consistent with prior in vitro studies implicating estrogen in melanin synthesis (McLeod et al., 1994; Ranson et al., 1988).
evidence: Supported by citations to McLeod et al., 1994 and Ranson et al., 1988.

claim: Most hormonal oral contraceptives incorporate ethinyl estradiol.
source: Hormonal oral contraceptives, most of which incorporate ethinyl estradiol, are associated with melasma (Resnik, 1967b).
evidence: This is general medical knowledge about oral contraceptive composition.

claim: Hormonal oral contraceptives are associated with melasma.
source: Hormonal oral contraceptives, most of which incorporate ethinyl estradiol, are associated with melasma (Resnik, 1967b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Resnik, 1967b.

claim: Ethinyl estradiol increased melanin to levels similar to those observed with native estrogen.
source: Ethinyl estradiol also increased melanin to levels similar to those observed with native estrogen.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Estrogen-treated organotypic skin displayed a threefold increase in melanin content after one week.
source: After one week, estrogen-treated skin displayed a threefold increase in melanin content (Figure 1B), without changes in melanocyte number or density (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Estrogen treatment does not change melanocyte number or density in organotypic skin.
source: After one week, estrogen-treated skin displayed a threefold increase in melanin content (Figure 1B), without changes in melanocyte number or density (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Estrogen effects in other tissue types are often counter-balanced by progesterone.
source: Estrogen effects in other tissue types are often counter-balanced by progesterone (Ismail et al., 2015), which also increases during pregnancy.
evidence: Supported by citation to Ismail et al., 2015.

claim: Progesterone increases during pregnancy.
source: Estrogen effects in other tissue types are often counter-balanced by progesterone (Ismail et al., 2015), which also increases during pregnancy.
evidence: This is established medical knowledge about pregnancy hormones.

claim: 500 nM progesterone decreased melanin production by half (58% ± 11.4%) in culture.
source: At 500 nM, a concentration observed in third trimester pregnancy (Abbassi-Ghanavati et al., 2009), progesterone decreased melanin production by half (58% +/- 11.4%), both in culture (Figure 1D) and in skin tissue (Figure 1E), without altering melanocyte cell number (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: 500 nM progesterone is a concentration observed in third trimester pregnancy.
source: At 500 nM, a concentration observed in third trimester pregnancy (Abbassi-Ghanavati et al., 2009), progesterone decreased melanin production by half (58% +/- 11.4%), both in culture (Figure 1D) and in skin tissue (Figure 1E), without altering melanocyte cell number (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by citation to Abbassi-Ghanavati et al., 2009.

claim: Progesterone treatment does not alter melanocyte cell number in organotypic skin.
source: At 500 nM, a concentration observed in third trimester pregnancy (Abbassi-Ghanavati et al., 2009), progesterone decreased melanin production by half (58% +/- 11.4%), both in culture (Figure 1D) and in skin tissue (Figure 1E), without altering melanocyte cell number (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Female iPS-derived melanocytes respond to estrogen and progesterone similarly to male foreskin melanocytes.
source: To determine whether female cells also responded similarly, we treated female iPS-derived melanocytes with estrogen and progesterone and noted responses similar to those observed with the male cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Melanocytes from adult facial skin respond to estrogen and progesterone similarly to foreskin melanocytes.
source: To determine whether melanocytes isolated from body sites other than foreskin also responded similarly to sex hormones, we treated melanocytes from adult facial skin with estrogen and progesterone and again observed responses that were similar to those observed with the foreskin melanocytes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Steroid hormones have variable effects on melanocyte proliferation in culture.
source: Consistent with other groups who have noted that steroid hormones have variable effects on melanocyte proliferation in culture (Im et al., 2002), we observed modest changes in proliferation when isolated primary cells were treated with estrogen or progesterone in vitro.
evidence: Supported by citation to Im et al., 2002 and experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A-B.

claim: Estrogen treated melanocytes tended to proliferate slightly slower.
source: Estrogen treated melanocytes tended to proliferate slightly slower, while progesterone treated cells tended to proliferate slightly faster (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Progesterone treated melanocytes tended to proliferate slightly faster.
source: Estrogen treated melanocytes tended to proliferate slightly slower, while progesterone treated cells tended to proliferate slightly faster (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Adult interfollicular epidermal melanocytes are relatively nonproliferative in vivo.
source: These proliferation changes are likely an in vitro artifact, as adult interfollicular epidermal melanocytes are relatively nonproliferative in vivo, and we did not note any changes in melanocyte numbers in sex steroid-treated 3-D organotypic tissues.
evidence: This is established knowledge about melanocyte behavior in vivo, and supported by the authors' observations in 3D organotypic tissues.

claim: Only 2 proliferative interfollicular melanocytes were identified in 280 tissue sections from normal human skin from 18 donors.
source: Consistent with this lack of melanocyte proliferation in interfollicular epidermis, another group thoroughly examined 280 tissue sections from normal human skin from 18 donors, and identified only 2 proliferative interfollicular melanocytes (Jimbow et al., 1975).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jimbow et al., 1975.

claim: Estrogen treatment increases cAMP in melanocytes.
source: To determine the mechanisms mediating estrogen and progesterone pigment effects, we examined components of the canonical pigment production pathway, and observed a cAMP increase upon estrogen treatment (Figure 2A), suggesting that estrogen accesses the canonical pigment production pathway downstream of MC1R.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Estrogen accesses the canonical pigment production pathway downstream of MC1R.
source: To determine the mechanisms mediating estrogen and progesterone pigment effects, we examined components of the canonical pigment production pathway, and observed a cAMP increase upon estrogen treatment (Figure 2A), suggesting that estrogen accesses the canonical pigment production pathway downstream of MC1R.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that estrogen increases cAMP.

claim: Estrogen treatment induces pCREB and MITF proteins.
source: Consistent with this, pCREB and MITF proteins were similarly induced (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Progesterone decreases cAMP in melanocytes.
source: In contrast, progesterone reciprocally decreased melanin, cAMP, pCREB and MITF (Figures 2C–D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Progesterone decreases pCREB and MITF proteins.
source: In contrast, progesterone reciprocally decreased melanin, cAMP, pCREB and MITF (Figures 2C–D).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Estrogen, progesterone, and αMSH converge on adenylate cyclase to reciprocally modulate melanin synthesis.
source: These data indicate that estrogen, progesterone, and αMSH converge on adenylate cyclase to reciprocally modulate melanin synthesis, and suggest that individual steroid effects may counter-balance each other.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cAMP data and knowledge of the melanin synthesis pathway.

claim: Individual steroid effects may counter-balance each other.
source: These data indicate that estrogen, progesterone, and αMSH converge on adenylate cyclase to reciprocally modulate melanin synthesis, and suggest that individual steroid effects may counter-balance each other.
evidence: This is an inference based on the reciprocal effects of estrogen and progesterone.

claim: Estrogen effects are significantly attenuated in the presence of progesterone.
source: Consistent with this, the estrogen effects were significantly attenuated in the presence of progesterone (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Pregnancy-associated hyperpigmentation is characteristically limited to specific areas where melanocyte or UV radiation exposure is highest including the face, genital, and areolar regions.
source: This likely helps explain why pregnancy-associated hyperpigmentation is characteristically limited to specific areas where melanocyte or UV radiation exposure is highest including the face, genital, and areolar regions (Szabo, 1954; Staricco and Pinkus, 1957).
evidence: Supported by citations to Szabo, 1954 and Staricco and Pinkus, 1957.

claim: MC1R is a G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR).
source: Considering MC1R is a G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR), we hypothesized that alternative GPCRs mediate sex steroid pigment effects.
evidence: This is established knowledge about MC1R.

claim: 61 distinct GPCRs are expressed in melanocytes out of 412 known or predicted 7-pass human GPCRs.
source: To identify possible candidates, we analyzed whole transcriptome melanocyte RNAseq data. Of 412 known or predicted 7-pass human GPCRs (Alexander et al., 2013), 61 distinct GPCRs were expressed in MCs, including the membrane-bound, G protein-coupled estrogen receptor (Filardo et al., 2002) (GPER) (Figure 2—source data 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data analysis shown in Figure 2—source data 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: GPER is expressed in melanocytes.
source: Of 412 known or predicted 7-pass human GPCRs (Alexander et al., 2013), 61 distinct GPCRs were expressed in MCs, including the membrane-bound, G protein-coupled estrogen receptor (Filardo et al., 2002) (GPER) (Figure 2—source data 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and qRT-PCR in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Estrogen binding to GPER modulates cAMP in breast cancer cell lines and fish oocytes.
source: Given that prior work in breast cancer cell lines and fish oocytes determined that estrogen binding to GPER modulates cAMP (Filardo et al., 2002; Thomas et al., 2005; Cabas et al., 2013; Majumder et al., 2015; Pang and Thomas, 2010), and that cAMP signaling stimulates melanin synthesis, we thought it possible that GPER may be the physiologically relevant human melanocyte estrogen receptor.
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies on GPER function.

claim: PAQR7 is expressed in melanocytes.
source: The melanocyte RNAseq studies also demonstrated that an analogous, noncanonical G protein-coupled progesterone receptor, progestin and adipoQ receptor 7 (PAQR7) (Zhu et al., 2003; Tang et al., 2005), was also expressed (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and qRT-PCR in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: GPER expression is markedly lower in keratinocytes and fibroblasts compared to melanocytes.
source: Notably, GPER and PAQR7 expression was markedly lower in other skin cells including keratinocytes and fibroblasts (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: PAQR7 expression is markedly lower in keratinocytes and fibroblasts compared to melanocytes.
source: Notably, GPER and PAQR7 expression was markedly lower in other skin cells including keratinocytes and fibroblasts (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: shRNA-mediated GPER depletion completely eliminated the melanocyte pigmentation response to estrogen.
source: To establish the necessity of GPER and PAQR7 in mediating sex hormone effects in MCs, we first depleted GPER using either of two independent shRNA hairpins, which completely eliminated the melanocyte pigmentation response to estrogen (Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E–F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E-F.

claim: shRNA-mediated PAQR7 depletion ablated the pigmentary response to progesterone.
source: Analogous shRNA-mediated PAQR7 depletion ablated the pigmentary response to progesterone (Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: CRISPR-Cas9 mediated gene disruption of GPER completely blocked the pigmentary response to estrogen.
source: To verify these results, we next used a complementary genetic approach based on CRISPR-Cas9 mediated gene disruption of GPER or PAQR7, which also completely blocked the pigmentary response to estrogen and progesterone, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G–H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G.

claim: CRISPR-Cas9 mediated gene disruption of PAQR7 completely blocked the pigmentary response to progesterone.
source: To verify these results, we next used a complementary genetic approach based on CRISPR-Cas9 mediated gene disruption of GPER or PAQR7, which also completely blocked the pigmentary response to estrogen and progesterone, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G–H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1H.

claim: PAQR7 was found to bind progesterone and regulate the final stages of sea trout oocyte meiosis through cAMP reduction.
source: Consistent with our model in which these receptors access melanin synthesis at the level of adenylate cyclase, PAQR7 was found to bind progesterone and regulate the final stages of sea trout oocyte meiosis through cAMP reduction (Zhu et al., 2003; Tokumoto et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Zhu et al., 2003 and Tokumoto et al., 2012.

claim: PAQR7 signals through G protein complexes containing the inhibitory G subunit (Gi) in fish oocytes.
source: In that fish system, PAQR7 signals through G protein complexes containing the inhibitory G subunit (Gi), which represses adenylate cyclase.
evidence: This is knowledge from the fish oocyte system cited earlier.

claim: Pertussis toxin (PTX) specifically inactivates Gi subunits via ADP-ribosylation.
source: To examine whether this signaling mechanism is functional in melanocytes, we treated melanocytes with progesterone in the presence of pertussis toxin (PTX), an exotoxin that specifically inactivates Gi subunits via ADP-ribosylation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PTX mechanism of action.

claim: PTX treatment alone results in a small increase in melanin production.
source: With PTX treatment alone, we observed a small increase in melanin production.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: PTX blocked progesterone effects on melanin production.
source: Importantly, PTX blocked progesterone effects, establishing that progesterone signals through Gi subunits (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Progesterone signals through Gi subunits in melanocytes.
source: Importantly, PTX blocked progesterone effects, establishing that progesterone signals through Gi subunits (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the PTX blocking experiment.

claim: Tamoxifen is associated with melasma in breast cancer patients.
source: Tamoxifen, an ER antagonist, is associated with melasma in breast cancer patients (Kim and Yoon, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kim and Yoon, 2009.

claim: Tamoxifen is a GPER agonist.
source: However, tamoxifen is a GPER agonist (Thomas et al., 2005; Li et al., 2010), and increased melanin to levels comparable to those observed with estrogen (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by citations to Thomas et al., 2005 and Li et al., 2010.

claim: Tamoxifen increased melanin to levels comparable to those observed with estrogen.
source: However, tamoxifen is a GPER agonist (Thomas et al., 2005; Li et al., 2010), and increased melanin to levels comparable to those observed with estrogen (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: G-1 is a specific GPER agonist that does not bind ER.
source: To determine whether GPER signaling was sufficient to increase melanin, we utilized the specific GPER agonist G-1 (Bologa et al., 2006), an estrogen analog developed for mechanistic studies in other systems that does not bind ER.
evidence: Supported by citation to Bologa et al., 2006.

claim: G-1 drove a dose-dependent increase in melanin production through pCREB and MITF that was GPER dependent.
source: G-1 drove a dose-dependent increase in melanin production through pCREB and MITF that was GPER dependent (Figure 3A–C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A-C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-D.

claim: G-1 and estrogen effects were blocked by GPER antagonists G-15 and G-36.
source: Further establishing that GPER is the melanocyte estrogen receptor, G-1 and estrogen effects were blocked by either of two specific GPER antagonists, G-15 and G-36 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E), which do not have inhibitory activity against ER (Dennis et al., 2009; 2011).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2E.

claim: G-15 and G-36 do not have inhibitory activity against ER.
source: Further establishing that GPER is the melanocyte estrogen receptor, G-1 and estrogen effects were blocked by either of two specific GPER antagonists, G-15 and G-36 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E), which do not have inhibitory activity against ER (Dennis et al., 2009; 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dennis et al., 2009 and 2011.

claim: Org OD-02 (CH2P4) is a specific PAQR7 agonist that does not bind PR.
source: To establish that PAQR7 signaling is sufficient to decrease melanin production, we used a specific PAQR7 agonist Org OD-02 (CH2P4), which does not bind PR (Kelder et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kelder et al., 2010.

claim: CH2P4 caused a dose-dependent decrease in melanin production through pCREB and MITF that was PAQR7 dependent.
source: CH2P4 caused a dose-dependent decrease in melanin production through pCREB and MITF that was PAQR7 dependent (Figure 3D–F and Figure 3—figure supplement 3A–D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D-F and Figure 3—figure supplement 3A-D.

claim: Topical application of 2% (w/v) G-1 in DMSO to mouse ears for 3 weeks resulted in a gradual increase in pigmentation.
source: We treated the right ears of mice daily for 3 weeks with vehicle or 2% (w/v) G-1 in DMSO, and observed a gradual increase pigmentation compared to vehicle-treated controls over 3 weeks (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Topical G-1 treatment increased melanin content 1.6-fold in mouse ears.
source: Melanin content was increased 1.6-fold, a cosmetically significant change, and was consistent with the magnitude of change seen in vitro (Figure 4B–C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B-C.

claim: Safe and effective approaches for modulating skin melanocyte function for therapeutic benefit are lacking.
source: Safe and effective approaches for modulating skin melanocyte function for therapeutic benefit are lacking, largely because the factors normally regulating melanocyte homeostasis are complex and incompletely deciphered.
evidence: This is a general statement about the state of the field.

claim: Myriad genetic and acquired conditions including acne, eczema, vitiligo, UV radiation exposure, traumatic injury, and pregnancy are associated with alterations in skin pigmentation.
source: Defining these mechanisms is important however, as myriad genetic and acquired conditions including common afflictions such as acne, eczema, vitiligo, ultraviolet (UV) radiation exposure, traumatic injury, and pregnancy are associated with alterations in skin pigmentation that can be extensive and long-lasting (James et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to James et al., 2011.

claim: People with naturally light skin, especially those with red hair, have a markedly decreased ability to synthesize UV-protective brown eumelanin as a result of inactivating mutations in MC1R.
source: Another population that could potentially benefit from modulating skin pigment are people with naturally light skin, especially those with red hair, who have a markedly decreased ability to synthesize UV-protective brown eumelanin as a result of inactivating mutations in MC1R (Valverde et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citation to Valverde et al., 1995.

claim: People with inactivating MC1R mutations are especially susceptible to photodamage, sunburns, and have an increased lifetime risk of keratinocyte and melanocyte-derived skin cancers.
source: This large population is especially susceptible to photodamage, sunburns, and has an increased lifetime risk of keratinocyte and melanocyte-derived skin cancers (Han et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Han et al., 2006.

claim: There is currently no available therapeutic that promotes protective eumelanin pigment production.
source: There is currently no available therapeutic that promotes protective eumelanin pigment production.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of therapeutics.

claim: Specific activation of GPER bypasses MC1R to stimulate melanin synthesis.
source: However, the specific activation of GPER alternatively activates cAMP signaling, bypassing MC1R, to stimulate melanin synthesis, and could therefore be especially useful in this sun-vulnerable population.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings about GPER signaling.

claim: The only method currently available to increase skin melanin is UV exposure.
source: The only method currently available to increase skin melanin is UV exposure.
evidence: This is a statement about current methods for increasing melanin.

claim: UV exposure promotes premature aging, wrinkles, and skin cancer.
source: While effective at darkening skin, the requisite DNA damage promotes premature aging, wrinkles, and skin cancer.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the harmful effects of UV exposure.

claim: Commonly utilized approaches for decreasing skin melanin involve application of toxic mercury or arsenic compounds, especially common in India, China, Japan, and Korea.
source: Commonly utilized approaches for decreasing skin melanin are also often unsafe, and involve application of toxic mercury or arsenic compounds, especially common in India, China, Japan, and Korea, but also encountered in the U.S., and recently highlighted in a report from the California Department of Public Health (Report #14–046, 2014), or hydroquinone, a tyrosinase inhibitor, which has been banned in Europe because of concerns regarding its possible association with cancer (McGregor, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to California Department of Public Health report.

claim: Hydroquinone has been banned in Europe because of concerns regarding its possible association with cancer.
source: Commonly utilized approaches for decreasing skin melanin are also often unsafe, and involve application of toxic mercury or arsenic compounds, especially common in India, China, Japan, and Korea, but also encountered in the U.S., and recently highlighted in a report from the California Department of Public Health (Report #14–046, 2014), or hydroquinone, a tyrosinase inhibitor, which has been banned in Europe because of concerns regarding its possible association with cancer (McGregor, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to McGregor, 2007.

claim: GPER is expressed in the reproductive, nervous, cardiovascular, renal, pancreas, and immune systems.
source: GPER has been identified in the reproductive, nervous, cardiovascular, renal, pancreas, and immune systems (Prossnitz and Barton, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Prossnitz and Barton, 2011.

claim: GPER expression on T cells plays a role in 17β-estradiol-induced thymic atrophy and autoimmune encephalomyelitis.
source: In immune cells, GPER expression on T cells has been shown to play a role in 17β-estradiol-induced thymic atrophy and autoimmune encephalomyelitis.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from the literature.

claim: PAQR7 is expressed in the reproductive and nervous systems.
source: PAQR7 is expressed in the reproductive and nervous systems (Tokumoto et al., 2016), and in murine macrophages (Lu et al., 2015) and in human T cells (Dosiou et al., 2008), although the functional role of PAQR7 in those tissues remains relatively unclear.
evidence: Supported by citations to Tokumoto et al., 2016, Lu et al., 2015, and Dosiou et al., 2008.

claim: PAQR7 is expressed in murine macrophages and human T cells.
source: PAQR7 is expressed in the reproductive and nervous systems (Tokumoto et al., 2016), and in murine macrophages (Lu et al., 2015) and in human T cells (Dosiou et al., 2008), although the functional role of PAQR7 in those tissues remains relatively unclear.
evidence: Supported by citations to Lu et al., 2015 and Dosiou et al., 2008.

claim: PAQR7 is the first example of a melanocyte cellular signaling cascade that actively represses melanin synthesis at the level of G-protein signaling.
source: The finding that PAQR7 works through inhibitory Gi subunits is especially interesting, as it is the first example of a melanocyte cellular signaling cascade that actively represses melanin synthesis at the level of G-protein signaling, as opposed to classically defined pigment control mechanisms that modulate the strength of the stimulatory MC1R signal.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the PAQR7 mechanism based on the authors' findings.

claim: The Agouti protein decreases pigment production via physically binding to MC1R and inhibiting αMSH stimulation.
source: In many animal systems, the Agouti protein decreases pigment production via physically binding to MC1R and inhibiting αMSH stimulation (Ollmann et al., 1998), rather than through an actively suppressive mechanism.
evidence: Supported by citation to Ollmann et al., 1998.

claim: A prior report claimed that normal primary melanocytes express nuclear ER or PR.
source: Our finding that normal primary melanocytes lack nuclear ER or PR contradicts a prior report (Im et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a reference to a contradictory finding in the literature.

claim: Melanocyte protein extracts have the ability to bind radioactive estrogen.
source: Another group demonstrated that melanocyte protein extracts have the ability to bind radioactive estrogen, but that work did not identify the specific protein(s) responsible for the binding activity (Jee et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jee et al., 1994.

claim: In some tissue settings, including neoplastic lesions and possibly hair follicles, melanocytes may express nuclear ER/PR.
source: We do not exclude the possibility that in some tissue settings, including neoplastic lesions and possibly hair follicles, melanocytes express nuclear ER/PR.
evidence: This is a speculative statement acknowledging possible exceptions.

claim: There is no known direct signaling pathway linking nuclear sex hormone receptors to the melanin synthesis machinery.
source: Still, as there is no known direct signaling pathway linking nuclear sex hormone receptors to the melanin synthesis machinery, it is most likely that the major effects of estrogen and progesterone on pigment production are mediated through the Gs and Gi coupled GPCRs identified in our current work.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Melanocytes express histamine and leukotriene receptors.
source: While surveying all the 7-pass transmembrane proteins expressed in melanocytes, we noted expression of several additional receptors that may also influence melanin production. These include histamine (Yoshida et al., 2000; Lassalle et al., 2003) and leukotriene receptors, which in other contexts are known to signal through Gs and Gi subunits (Mondillo et al., 2005; Arcemisbéhère et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Histamine and leukotriene receptors signal through Gs and Gi subunits in other contexts.
source: These include histamine (Yoshida et al., 2000; Lassalle et al., 2003) and leukotriene receptors, which in other contexts are known to signal through Gs and Gi subunits (Mondillo et al., 2005; Arcemisbéhère et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mondillo et al., 2005 and Arcemisbéhère et al., 2010.

claim: G-1 was synthesized to 95% purity.
source: To demonstrate that GPER was sufficient to promote melanin production in vivo, we synthesized G-1 to 95% purity (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B), and formulated G-1 for topical application.
evidence: Supported by NMR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B.
